**My call: don't build them "anyway" — but don't park the problem either. Rework a slimmer package and put it back to voters, with extra lanes only at the genuinely worst bottlenecks.** Ignoring the referendum would be the wrong decision; doing nothing would also be the wrong decision.

Why not just proceed anyway: a 52.7% No (despite the cantons barely squeaking out a yes) isn't a landslide, but it is a mandate against that specific plan. Quietly overriding it would poison trust in direct democracy — the very thing that makes Swiss infrastructure decisions durable. Rejected proposals get reworked and re-voted all the time; that's the legitimate route, and given how narrow the result was, a revised version has a fair shot.

Why I still lean toward building *something*: the costs of the status quo are real — on the order of a billion francs a year in lost time, more crashes in stop-and-go, unreliable freight. The No campaign largely objected to the package's size and "roads-first" framing, not to every meter of asphalt. And rail can't absorb it all: Bern–Zurich trains are genuinely good, but Zurich's rail node is near its ceiling, and the next big rail fix costs tens of billions over decades.

The honest caveat: induced demand. In congested corridors, a large share of any added capacity refills within a few years. Lanes alone are a weak answer — they only work bundled with flow management.

What I'd actually do:

- **Temporary hard-shoulder running at peak** on the worst A1 stretches — cheap, fast, reversible, worth 15–20% capacity in trials. Doesn't require the rejected decree and could start tomorrow.
- **More ramp metering and speed harmonization** to keep traffic flowing instead of the accordion effect.
- **Extra lanes only where a chronic bottleneck demonstrably exists** — likely a handful of kilometers, not the full ~5-billion package.
- **Pair it explicitly with the rail package** (and the climate targets) so it's not framed as roads versus climate.
- **Then a second referendum** on the trimmed version.

That's my judgment: build *some* of it, but earn the mandate again rather than bypassing the last one. Neither ideology — "no asphalt ever" nor "concrete fixes everything" — will actually fix your commute; a narrower, better-evidenced version probably helps more than either.
